title: POUM leaders involved in the 1934 revolt in Spain
summary: Several POUM leaders had revolutionary histories that included involvement in the 1934 Spanish revolt, undermining Communist charges that the POUM was a Fascist organization.

citation.quote: All the POUM leaders had revolutionary histories behind them. Some of them had been mixed up in the 1934 revolt, and most of them had been imprisoned for Socialist activities under the Lerroux Government or the monarchy.

title: Government troops storm Mount Aragón fortress
summary: Republican government forces captured the medieval fortress of Mount Aragón, which guarded an approach to Huesca, reportedly for the first time in the fortress's history.

citation.quote: Mount Aragón, the medieval fortress which the Government troops had stormed last year (the first time in its history, it was said), and which guarded one of the approaches to Huesca, there was a heavy gun which must have dated well back into the nineteenth century.

title: Joaquín Maurín warns the Cortes of Franco's impending revolt
summary: In 1936 Joaquín Maurín, then leader of the POUM, was one of the deputies who gave warning in the Spanish Cortes of Franco's impending revolt, further contradicting the Communist charge that the POUM was in Fascist pay.

citation.quote: In 1936 its then leader, Joaquín Maurín, was one of the deputies who gave warning in the Cortes of Franco's impending revolt.

title: Spanish Civil War fighting breaks out
summary: Armed fighting erupts in Spain on 18 July 1936, prompting anti-Fascists across Europe to see it as democracy finally standing up to Fascism after years of appeasement.

citation.quote: When the fighting broke out on 18 July it is probable that every anti-Fascist in Europe felt a thrill of hope. For here at last, apparently, was democracy standing up to Fascism.

title: Government troops begin long siege of Saragossa
summary: Republican militia forces took up positions outside Saragossa in August 1936 and were still holding the same line when Orwell arrived, having made no advance on the city.

citation.quote: The Government troops had gazed at it from that distance since August 1936, and they are gazing at it still.

title: Daily Worker attacks those claiming Spain is fighting for social revolution
summary: The Daily Worker declared that those who said the Spanish people were fighting for social revolution, rather than bourgeois democracy, were 'downright lying scoundrels'.

citation.quote: According to the Daily Worker (6 August 1936) those who said that the Spanish people were fighting for social revolution, or for anything other than bourgeois democracy, were 'downright lying scoundrels'.

title: Anarchists capture Siétamo after three engagements
summary: The town of Siétamo, on the Aragon front, changed hands multiple times before Anarchist militia forces finally took it in October 1936. Shell-fire and rifle-fire left parts of the town in ruins.

citation.quote: Siétamo had been fought over three times before the Anarchists finally took it in October, and parts of it were smashed to pieces by shell-fire and most of the houses pock-marked by rifle-bullets.

title: Savage fighting for hilltop positions around Saragossa
summary: Around October 1936 there was fierce fighting for the hilltops near Saragossa on the Aragón front. After this, both armies dug in on the positions they had won, stalling the front for months.

citation.quote: Earlier, about October, there had been savage fighting for all these hills; then, because the lack of men and arms, especially artillery, made any large-scale operation impossible, each army had dug itself in and settled down on the hill-tops it had won.

title: Bob Smillie arrives in Spain
summary: Bob Smillie arrived in Spain in October 1936 and worked for several months at the POUM office before joining the militia when other ILP members arrived.

citation.quote: Smillie had been in Spain since the previous October. He had worked for several months at the POUM office and had then joined the militia when the other ILP members arrived, on the understanding that he was to do three months at the front before going back to England to take part in a propaganda tour.

title: Georges Kopp joins the POUM militia and enters the front line
summary: Georges Kopp had been serving on the front line since October 1936, having left Belgium and enlisted in the POUM militia despite facing legal consequences at home. By the time of his arrest in June 1937 he had risen from militiaman to major.

citation.quote: He had been in the line since October 1936, had worked his way up from militiaman to major, had been in action I do not know how many times, and had been wounded once.

title: USSR begins supplying arms to the Spanish Republic, shifting power from Anarchists to Communists
summary: From around October–November 1936, the USSR began supplying arms to the Spanish Government, allowing the Communists to dictate terms and triggering a general swing to the Right as power passed from the Anarchists.

citation.quote: The general swing to the Right dates from about October–November 1936, when the USSR began to supply arms to the Government and power began to pass from the Anarchists to the Communists.

title: Orwell arrives in Barcelona and joins the POUM militia
summary: George Orwell arrived in Barcelona intending to write newspaper articles but almost immediately enlisted in the POUM militia, drawn in by the revolutionary atmosphere of the city under Anarchist control.

citation.quote: This was in late December, 1936, less than seven months ago as I write, and yet it is a period that has already receded into enormous distance. Later events have obliterated it much more completely than they have obliterated 1935, or 1905, for that matter. I had come to Spain with some notion of writing newspaper articles, but I had joined the militia almost immediately, because at that time and in that atmosphere it seemed the only conceivable thing to do.

title: POUM militia column departs Lenin Barracks for the Aragón front
summary: After about a week of training at the Lenin Barracks in Barcelona, Orwell's POUM militia centuria was ordered to the front at two hours' notice and marched through the Ramblas before boarding a train to Aragón.

citation.quote: This was in late December, 1936, less than seven months ago as I write, and yet it is a period that has already receded into enormous distance.

title: Spanish Popular Army raised as non-political force
summary: At the beginning of 1937 the Spanish Republic raised the Popular Army, a non-political force organized along conventional military lines, to eventually replace the party militias on the fronts.

citation.quote: When the Popular Army, which was a 'non-political' army organized on more or less ordinary lines, was raised at the beginning of 1937, the party militias were theoretically incorporated in it.

title: Paris International Exposition in full swing
summary: When Orwell passed through Paris after leaving Spain in mid-1937, the Paris International Exposition was in full swing, though he and his companions managed to avoid visiting it.

citation.quote: And the Exhibition was in full swing, though we managed to avoid visiting it.

title: Orwell arrives on the Aragón front
summary: George Orwell joins the POUM militia on the Aragón front in January 1937, where he serves until May. The front near Saragossa is largely static, with both sides dug into hilltop positions.

citation.quote: I was on the Aragón front from January to May, and between January and late March little or nothing happened on that front, except at Teruel.

title: Fascist aeroplane drops newspapers announcing fall of Málaga
summary: A Fascist aircraft flew over POUM positions on the Aragón front and dropped copies of the Heraldo de Aragón reporting the fall of Málaga, delivering the news as a propaganda drop.

citation.quote: One day in February we saw a Fascist aeroplane approaching... out of it came tumbling not bombs but white glittering things that turned over and over in the air... They were copies of a Fascist newspaper, the Heraldo de Aragón, announcing the fall of Málaga.

title: Fascist abortive attack on POUM position to celebrate fall of Málaga
summary: On the night of the propaganda drop, Fascist forces opened heavy machine-gun fire on Orwell's position at Monte Trazo — not a genuine assault, but a celebratory demonstration marking Málaga's fall.

citation.quote: That night the Fascists made a sort of abortive attack. I was just getting down into kip, half dead with sleep, when there was a heavy stream of bullets overhead and someone shouted into the dug-out: 'They're attacking!'

title: Press falsely reports heroic English repulse of cavalry and tank attack
summary: A day or two after the Fascist demonstration, newspapers and radio broadcast wildly exaggerated accounts of a cavalry and tank assault on the POUM positions, which had been repelled by the heroic English — an account Orwell regarded as entirely fabricated.

citation.quote: A day or two later the newspapers and the radio published reports of a tremendous attack with cavalry and tanks (up a perpendicular hill-side!) which had been beaten off by the heroic English.

title: POUM troops leave Monte Trazo to join the siege of Huesca
summary: In mid-February 1937, Orwell and all POUM forces in the sector were transported fifty miles to take part in the army besieging Huesca, shifting the front from Monte Trazo to the outskirts of that city.

citation.quote: In mid-February we left Monte Trazo and were sent, together with all the POUM troops in this sector, to make a part of the army besieging Huesca.

title: Militias theoretically incorporated into Popular Army; POUM Lenin Division renamed 29th Division
summary: Since February 1937 all armed forces in Spain were nominally merged into the Popular Army on paper, with the POUM's Lenin Division redesignated the 29th Division, though little changed in practice on the Aragón front until June.

citation.quote: Since February the entire armed forces had theoretically been incorporated in the Popular Army, and the militias were, on paper, reconstructed along Popular Army lines, with differential pay-rates, gazetted rank, etc. etc. The POUM troops, for instance, previously called the Lenin Division, were now known as the 29th Division.

title: Juan López declares Spanish people are fighting for revolution, not democracy
summary: Juan López, a member of the Valencia Government, publicly declared in February 1937 that the Spanish people were shedding their blood not for the democratic Republic but for a revolution.

citation.quote: On the other hand, Juan López, a member of the Valencia Government, declared in February 1937 that 'the Spanish people are shedding their blood, not for the democratic Republic and its paper Constitution, but for…a revolution.'

title: Heavy fighting around Huesca
summary: In March 1937 there was heavy fighting around Huesca on the Aragón front, though Orwell personally played only a minor part in it.

citation.quote: In March there was heavy fighting round Huesca, but I personally played only a minor part in it.

title: First effective grenades appear at the front
summary: Until late March 1937 the POUM militia were equipped only with primitive and dangerous bombs; it was not until late March that Orwell first saw a grenade he considered worth throwing.

citation.quote: It was not till late March that I saw a bomb worth throwing.

title: Orwell wounded and hospitalized at Monflorite
summary: Orwell suffered a poisoned hand that required lancing and a sling, sending him to the casualty clearing station at Monflorite for ten days. During the stay, hospital workers stole his camera and photographs.

citation.quote: Towards the end of March I got a poisoned hand that had to be lanced and put in a sling. I had to go into hospital, but it was not worth sending me to Siétamo for such a petty injury, so I stayed in the so-called hospital at Monflorite, which was merely a casualty clearing station. I was there ten days, part of the time in bed.

title: Italian International Column wins victory at Guadalajara
summary: Italian troops serving in the International Column won a major victory at Guadalajara in March 1937, before being transferred to the Aragón front, where most were subsequently killed at Huesca.

citation.quote: We heard afterwards that these were some of the troops who won the great victory at Guadalajara in March; they had been on leave and were being transferred to the Aragón front.

title: POUM militia advances the line east of Huesca
summary: On Orwell's return from hospital in April, the POUM militia advanced their line roughly a thousand yards forward to a stream near the Fascist positions. Six hundred men dug 1,200 metres of trench in one night in near-total silence.

citation.quote: In seven hours six hundred men constructed twelve hundred metres of trench and parapet, at distances of from a hundred and fifty to three hundred yards from the Fascist line, and all so silently that the Fascists heard nothing, and during the night there was only one casualty. Though this was April it was the coldest night that I remember in Spain.

title: Anarchist attacks on the Jaca road near Huesca
summary: Anarchist forces launched a series of attacks on the Jaca road west of Huesca in April 1937. The POUM militia conducted holding attacks on the eastern side to force the Fascists to divert troops.

citation.quote: The point of doing it now was that the Anarchists were attacking on the Jaca road, and to advance on this side made them divert troops to face us.

title: Roldán Cortada, prominent UGT member, murdered in Barcelona
summary: At the end of April 1937, Roldán Cortada, a prominent member of the UGT, was murdered, presumably by someone in the CNT, intensifying the political tension between the two union federations.

citation.quote: At the end of April, just after I got to Barcelona, Roldán Cortada, a prominent member of the UGT, was murdered, presumably by someone in the CNT.

title: Government stages massive funeral procession for Roldán Cortada in Barcelona
summary: Following Cortada's murder, the Government ordered all shops to close and staged an enormous funeral procession composed largely of Popular Army troops, which took two hours to pass a given point — widely seen as a show of political strength.

citation.quote: The Government ordered all shops to close and staged an enormous funeral procession, largely of Popular Army troops, which took two hours to pass a given point. From the hotel window I watched it without enthusiasm. It was obvious that the so-called funeral was merely a display of strength.

title: Douglas Thompson wounded at the Aragón front
summary: Around the beginning of April 1937, fellow militiaman Douglas Thompson was wounded at the front and subsequently treated at Tarragona hospital before being sent back to Barcelona around the start of the May fighting.

citation.quote: I mentioned earlier that Douglas Thompson was wounded about the beginning of April. Afterwards we had lost touch with him, as usually happened when a man was wounded, for wounded men were frequently moved from one hospital to another. Actually he was at Tarragona hospital and was sent back to Barcelona about the time when the fighting started.

title: Orwell's section relieved and departs for Barcelona
summary: On 25 April another section relieved Orwell's unit at the front; they handed over their rifles and marched back to Monflorite, catching a train and arriving in Barcelona by the afternoon of the 26th.

citation.quote: On 25 April, after the usual mañanas, another section relieved us and we handed over our rifles, packed our kits and marched back to Monflorite.

title: Caballero Government falls, replaced by more right-wing government
summary: The Largo Caballero government collapsed and was succeeded by a more right-wing cabinet with stronger Communist influence, as Orwell had predicted would happen within weeks.

citation.quote: It was easy to see that the Caballero Government would fall and be replaced by a more Right-wing Government with a stronger Communist influence (this happened a week or two later), which would set itself to break the power of the trade unions once and for all.

title: Bob Smillie arrested at the Spanish frontier
summary: Bob Smillie was arrested at the frontier while attempting to return to England, taken to Valencia, and imprisoned on a pretext of carrying arms. Orwell believed the real reason was his connection to the POUM in the aftermath of the Barcelona fighting.

citation.quote: We had just reached the front when we heard that Bob Smillie, on his way back to England, had been arrested at the frontier, taken down to Valencia and thrown into jail.

title: Orwell shot by Fascist sniper at Huesca
summary: Orwell was shot through the throat by a Fascist sniper at the corner of the parapet at five o'clock in the morning, about ten days after returning to the front following the Barcelona fighting.

citation.quote: I had been about ten days at the front when it happened. The whole experience of being hit by a bullet is very interesting and I think it is worth describing in detail.

title: POUM joins the Barcelona street fighting alongside the CNT
summary: In May 1937 the POUM joined in the disastrous street fighting in Barcelona, acting mainly from an instinct to stand by the CNT.

citation.quote: When the POUM joined in the disastrous fighting in Barcelona in May, it was mainly from an instinct to stand by the CNT, and later, when the POUM was suppressed, the Anarchists were the only people who dared to raise a voice in its defence.

title: Tension in Catalonia reaches breaking point ahead of Barcelona fighting
summary: By May 1937 the struggle between Communists and Anarchists over arms, policing, and control of key industries had reached a point where violent conflict was regarded as inevitable.

citation.quote: By May 1937 things had reached a point at which some kind of violent outbreak could be regarded as inevitable.

title: Barcelona May Day demonstration called off; no celebrations held
summary: A planned joint CNT–UGT May Day demonstration in Barcelona was cancelled at the last moment due to fears of rioting, making Barcelona likely the only city in non-Fascist Europe with no May Day celebrations in 1937.

citation.quote: So nothing happened on 1 May. It was a queer state of affairs. Barcelona, the so-called revolutionary city, was probably the only city in non-Fascist Europe that had no celebrations that day.

title: May Day passes without rioting in Barcelona
summary: Many people in Barcelona were agreeably surprised when no rioting broke out on May Day 1937, given the high tension throughout Catalonia.

citation.quote: Many people were agreeably surprised when there was no rioting on 1 May.

title: First report of trouble at the Barcelona Telephone Exchange
summary: At midday on 3 May, Orwell first hears a casual report that something has gone wrong at the Telephone Exchange, though he pays no attention to it at the time.

citation.quote: About midday on 3 May a friend crossing the lounge of the hotel said casually: 'There's been some kind of trouble at the Telephone Exchange, I hear.' For some reason I paid no attention to it at the time.

title: Rifle fire erupts on the Ramblas as Barcelona street fighting begins
summary: On the afternoon of 3 May, between three and four o'clock, Orwell hears rifle shots on the Ramblas and witnesses Anarchist youth exchanging fire with gunmen in a church tower, marking the open outbreak of the May Days fighting.

citation.quote: That afternoon, between three and four, I was half-way down the Ramblas when I heard several rifle-shots behind me. I turned round and saw some youths, with rifles in their hands and the red and black handkerchiefs of the Anarchists round their throats, edging up a side-street that ran off the Ramblas northward.

title: Assault Guards storm the CNT-held Telephone Exchange
summary: On 3 May, several lorry-loads of Assault Guards drove to the Telephone Exchange, operated mainly by CNT workers, and launched a sudden assault on it, triggering the Barcelona street fighting.

citation.quote: It appeared that he had been in the Plaza de Cataluña when several lorry-loads of armed Assault Guards had driven up to the Telephone Exchange, which was operated mainly by CNT workers, and made a sudden assault upon it. Then some Anarchists had arrived and there had been a general affray.

title: Salas, Chief of Police, placed under arrest
summary: In the early hours of the morning following the outbreak of fighting, Orwell is told that Salas, the Chief of Police responsible for ordering the attack on the Telephone Exchange, has been placed under arrest, though he was later only deprived of his post.

citation.quote: At three in the morning the tall handsome man who seemed to be in command woke me up, gave me a rifle and put me on guard at one of the windows. He told me that Salas, the Chief of Police responsible for the attack on the Telephone Exchange, had been placed under arrest.

title: Assault Guards seize the office of La Batalla, the POUM newspaper
summary: At approximately the same time as the attack on the Telephone Exchange on 3 May, the Assault Guards raided and occupied the undefended office of La Batalla, the POUM's newspaper, though the paper continued to be printed from another address.

citation.quote: The office of *La Batalla*, the POUM paper, which was not defended, had been raided and seized by the Assault Guards at about the same time as the Telephone Exchange, but the paper was being printed, and a few copies distributed, from another address.

title: Government Assault Guards seize Barcelona Telephone Exchange, triggering street fighting
summary: On 3 May the Government sent three lorry-loads of armed Assault Guards to seize the CNT-operated Telephone Exchange, prompting armed Anarchists to take to the streets and igniting the Barcelona May Days fighting.

citation.quote: On 3 May the Government decided to take over the Telephone Exchange, which had been operated since the beginning of the war mainly by CNT workers… Salas, the Chief of Police… sent three lorry-loads of armed Assault Guards to seize the building… armed Anarchists appeared on the streets, work ceased, and fighting broke out immediately.

title: Solidaridad Obrera condemns attack on Telephone Exchange as monstrous provocation
summary: On Tuesday 4 May, the Anarchist newspaper Solidaridad Obrera described the government assault on the Telephone Exchange as a 'monstrous provocation,' reflecting the CNT's initial combative stance before it reversed course the following day.

citation.quote: On Tuesday *Solidaridad Obrera*, the Anarchist paper, had described the attack on the Telephone Exchange as a 'monstrous provocation' (or words to that effect), but on Wednesday it changed its tune and began imploring everyone to go back to work.

title: Douglas Thompson arrested and jailed during Barcelona street fighting
summary: On the Tuesday morning (4 May), Thompson returned to his hotel in an Assault Guard–controlled quarter; the hotel was raided and he was arrested and held for eight days in an overcrowded cell, one of many wrongful arrests made during the disturbances.

citation.quote: On the Tuesday morning I met him in the street, considerably bewildered by the firing that was going on all round...He went back to his hotel, but unfortunately...The place was raided and Thompson was arrested, flung into jail, and kept for eight days in a cell so full of people that nobody had room to lie down.

title: Trotskyist ('Bolshevik-Leninist') group issues handbill calling for general strike
summary: On 4 May a small group of Trotskyists issued a handbill calling for everyone to go to the barricades and for a general strike of all industries except war industries.

citation.quote: The only handbill I saw during the fighting was one issued by the tiny group of Trotskyists ('Bolshevik-Leninists') on 4 May. This merely said: 'Everyone to the barricades – general strike of all industries except war industries.'

title: Anarchist leaders and Solidaridad Obrera urge workers to abandon the barricades
summary: By Wednesday 5 May, Solidaridad Obrera reversed its position and began urging everyone to return to work, while Anarchist leaders simultaneously broadcast the same conciliatory message, signalling a collapse of resistance.

citation.quote: It was about Wednesday (5 May) that a change seemed to come over things...on Wednesday it changed its tune and began imploring everyone to go back to work. The Anarchist leaders were broadcasting the same message.

title: British destroyers observed closing in on Barcelona harbour
summary: On Wednesday 5 May, Orwell and fellow militiaman Douglas Moyle watched from the observatory tower as what turned out to be British destroyers moved into Barcelona harbour, later confirmed to be true though not understood at the time.

citation.quote: Watching from the observatory tower we saw the low grey shapes of warships closing in upon the harbour. Douglas Moyle, who had been a sailor, said that they looked like British destroyers. As a matter of fact they *were* British destroyers, though we did not learn this till afterwards.

title: Four hundred Assault Guards surrender their arms to Anarchists at Plaza de España
summary: On the evening of 5 May, Orwell hears that four hundred Assault Guards on the Plaza de España had surrendered and handed their weapons to the Anarchists, and that the CNT appeared to be in control of the suburbs.

citation.quote: That evening we heard that on the Plaza de España four hundred Assault Guards had surrendered and handed their arms to the Anarchists; also the news was vaguely filtering through that in the suburbs (mainly working-class quarters) the CNT were in control.

title: Kopp warns that the Valencia Government is about to outlaw the POUM
summary: On the evening of 5 May, Georges Kopp gravely informed Orwell that the Government was reportedly about to declare the POUM an illegal organisation and open war upon it, forcing POUM fighters to prepare to defend their buildings.

citation.quote: But the same evening Kopp sent for me and, with a grave face, told me that according to information he had just received the Government was about to outlaw the POUM and declare a state of war upon it.

title: Friends of Durruti distribute revolutionary leaflet during Barcelona fighting
summary: The Friends of Durruti, a small extremist group within the FAI, distributed a revolutionary leaflet on 5 May calling for a revolutionary council, the shooting of those responsible for the attack on the Telephone Exchange, and the disarming of the Assault Guards.

citation.quote: The Friends of Durruti distributed some kind of revolutionary leaflet, but this did not appear until 5 May and cannot be said to have started the fighting, which had started of its own accord two days earlier.

title: Armistice declared in Barcelona street fighting; POUM's La Batalla endorses Friends of Durruti leaflet
summary: On 6 May an armistice was declared in the Barcelona fighting, though combat soon broke out again. The same day POUM's newspaper La Batalla expressed approval of the Friends of Durruti leaflet.

citation.quote: On 6 May there was an armistice, but fighting soon broke out again, probably because of premature attempts by Assault Guards to disarm CNT workers.

title: Valencian Assault Guards arrive in Barcelona to restore government control
summary: On the Friday evening (7 May), well-armed Valencian Assault Guards suddenly appeared throughout Barcelona's streets in groups of ten, making a show of force to overawe the population and effectively ending the May Days fighting.

citation.quote: I spent that final night on the roof, and the next day it did really look as though the fighting was coming to an end. I do not think there was much firing that day – the Friday. No one seemed to know for certain whether the troops from Valencia were really coming; they arrived that evening, as a matter of fact.

title: Six thousand Assault Guards arrive from Valencia; Barcelona May Days fighting ends
summary: By the afternoon of 7 May conditions in Barcelona were almost normal. That evening six thousand Assault Guards sent by sea from Valencia arrived and took control of the city, ending the May Days fighting.

citation.quote: By the afternoon of 7 May conditions were almost normal. That evening six thousand Assault Guards, sent by sea from Valencia, arrived and took control of the town.

title: Disastrous Republican attack on Huesca
summary: In June 1937 a disastrous Republican attack on Huesca resulted in several thousand men killed in a single day. Orwell had been wounded and disabled before this attack occurred.

citation.quote: Later, in June, there was the disastrous attack on Huesca in which several thousand men were killed in a single day, but I had been wounded and disabled before that happened.

title: Popular Army troops arrive on Aragón front in numbers
summary: New Popular Army troops did not reach the Aragón front in significant numbers until June 1937, meaning the militia system remained effectively unchanged on that front until then.

citation.quote: the new Popular Army troops did not reach the Aragón front in any numbers till June, and until that time the militia-system remained unchanged.

title: Government concentrates 30,000 troops on Huesca but fails to take the city
summary: The Republican Government transferred troops from the Madrid front and massed thirty thousand men with a large number of aeroplanes against Huesca in June 1937, but the city still did not fall.

citation.quote: Later, in June, the Government brought troops from the Madrid front and concentrated thirty thousand men on Huesca, with an enormous quantity of aeroplanes, but still the town did not fall.

title: Aragón front militia system radically altered
summary: The workers' militia system on the Aragón front, which had kept revolutionary sentiment concentrated among its ranks, was not radically changed until around June 1937.

citation.quote: This was the result of the militia-system, which on the Aragón front was not radically altered till about June 1937.

title: Italian troops killed at Huesca after Guadalajara victory
summary: Most of the Italian International Column troops seen passing through Tarragona were killed at Huesca only a few weeks after their transfer to the Aragón front.

citation.quote: Most of them, I am afraid, were killed at Huesca only a few weeks later.

title: Battle around the Jaca road resumes
summary: After a lull following earlier fighting, the battle around the Jaca road on the Aragón front resumed in mid-June 1937.

citation.quote: The battle round the Jaca road had died away and did not begin again till mid-June.

title: General José Rovira arrested near the front line
summary: About the end of June 1937, Barcelona police arrested General José Rovira, commander of the 29th Division, near the front line without informing either the Ministry of War or the Chief of Police. His troops sent a delegation to protest at the Ministry of War.

citation.quote: About the end of June José Rovira, the general commanding the 29th Division, was arrested somewhere near the front line by a party of police who had been sent from Barcelona.

title: Orwell and his wife cross the Spanish frontier into France
summary: After evading arrest in Barcelona for several days following the POUM suppression, Orwell and his wife crossed the frontier into France at Cerbères, returning to French soil after approximately six months in Spain.

citation.quote: So we slipped through the barrier, and after just six months I was on French soil again.

title: Kopp departs for Valencia and Orwell leaves for Siétamo
summary: Georges Kopp left for Valencia for an interview at the Ministry of War while Orwell simultaneously departed for Siétamo to obtain his discharge papers from the POUM militia headquarters.

citation.quote: He left for Valencia the same day as I left for Siétamo – 15 June.

title: Police arrest POUM leader Andrés Nin in Barcelona
summary: On the evening of 15 June 1937, Barcelona police suddenly arrested Andrés Nin at his office, initiating a broader crackdown on the POUM. Nin was subsequently transferred to Valencia and then Madrid, and was almost certainly killed in secret police custody.

citation.quote: On 15 June the police had suddenly arrested Andrés Nin in his office, and the same evening had raided the Hotel Falcón and arrested all the people in it, mostly militiamen on leave.

title: Police raid Hotel Falcón and arrest POUM militiamen on leave
summary: The same evening Nin was arrested, police raided the Hotel Falcón in Barcelona, arresting all occupants — mostly POUM militiamen on leave — and converting the hotel into a prison that rapidly filled with detainees.

citation.quote: On 15 June the police had suddenly arrested Andrés Nin in his office, and the same evening had raided the Hotel Falcón and arrested all the people in it, mostly militiamen on leave. The place was converted immediately into a prison, and in a very little while it was filled to the brim with prisoners of all kinds.

title: POUM suppressed and declared an illegal organization
summary: On 15–16 June 1937 the POUM was suppressed and declared illegal, one of the first acts of the Negrín Government. The Executive Committee of the POUM was thrown into jail.

citation.quote: Finally, on 15–16 June, the POUM was suppressed and declared an illegal organization. This was one of the first acts of the Negrín Government which came into office in May.

title: POUM declared an illegal organization; offices and sanatoria seized
summary: The day after Nin's arrest, the Spanish government declared the POUM an illegal organization and seized all its offices, bookstalls, sanatoria, and Red Aid centres. Within days, nearly all forty members of the POUM Executive Committee were imprisoned.

citation.quote: Next day the POUM was declared an illegal organization and all its offices, bookstalls, sanatoria, Red Aid centres and so forth were seized.

title: Kurt Landau and wife arrested; Landau disappears
summary: Kurt Landau and his wife were arrested around 17 June 1937 in Barcelona. Landau immediately vanished — his wife remained imprisoned for five months without trial or news of her husband, and was eventually informed by the Minister of Justice that he was dead.

citation.quote: They were arrested about 17 June, and Landau immediately 'disappeared'. Five months later his wife was still in jail, untried and without news of her husband.

title: Rumour reaches Barcelona that Nin has been shot
summary: As early as 21 June 1937, rumours reached Barcelona that Andrés Nin had been shot after his transfer to Valencia and then Madrid. The rumour later became more specific — that Nin had been killed by the secret police and his body dumped in the street — and Nin was never heard of alive again.

citation.quote: as early as 21 June the rumour reached Barcelona that he had been shot. Later the rumour took a more definite shape: Nin had been shot in prison by the secret police and his body dumped into the street.

title: Daily Worker publishes claims of vast POUM Fascist espionage plot
summary: On 21 June the Daily Worker, summarizing Spanish Communist papers, published sensational claims that arrested POUM leaders had confessed to transmitting military secrets to Franco by radio and acting in collaboration with a Fascist organization in Madrid.

citation.quote: For a while the Communist Press of the whole world was flaming with this kind of thing (*Daily Worker*, 21 June, summarizing various Spanish Communist papers):

title: Spanish churches remain closed to services under Republican government
summary: Until about July 1937, no churches in Republican Spain were allowed to reopen and hold services, with the exception of one or two Protestant churches in Madrid.

citation.quote: In six months in Spain I only saw two undamaged churches, and until about July 1937 no churches were allowed to reopen and hold services, except for one or two Protestant churches in Madrid.

title: Maxton delegation visits Spain to investigate charges against POUM and disappearance of Nin
summary: In August an international delegation headed by James Maxton MP went to Spain to inquire into the charges against the POUM and the disappearance of Andrés Nin. Multiple Spanish ministers repudiated belief in the espionage charges.

citation.quote: In August an international delegation headed by James Maxton, MP, went to Spain to inquire into the charges against the POUM and the disappearance of Andrés Nin.

title: New Statesman publishes accounts of Fascist barricades made of living children
summary: As late as October 1937 the New Statesman was still publishing sensationalist atrocity tales about the Spanish war, including stories of Fascist barricades made of the bodies of living children.

citation.quote: As late as October 1937 the New Statesman was treating us to tales of Fascist barricades made of the bodies of living children (a most unhandy thing to make barricades with), and Mr Arthur Bryant was declaring that 'the sawing-off of a Conservative tradesman's legs' was 'a commonplace' in Loyalist Spain.

title: Negrín publicly declares 'we respect private property'
summary: By the autumn of 1937, the 'Socialist' Prime Minister Negrín was making public speeches declaring 'we respect private property', reflecting the full rightward swing of the Republican government.

citation.quote: By the autumn of 1937 the 'Socialist' Negrín was declaring in public speeches that 'we respect private property,' and members of the Cortes who at the beginning of the war had had to fly the country because of their suspected Fascist sympathies were returning to Spain.

title: Duchess of Atholl's article in the Sunday Express describes order in wartime Spain
summary: The Duchess of Atholl published a piece in the Sunday Express claiming perfect order prevailed in Valencia, Madrid, and Barcelona, with comfortable hotels despite minor food shortages. Orwell cites this as evidence of how English visitors failed to see the repression around them.

citation.quote: The Duchess of Atholl writes, I notice (*Sunday Express*, 17 October 1937):

title: McGovern delegation visits Spain; minister confirms Communist control of police
summary: In December a delegation headed by John McGovern MP visited Spain and received similar answers to the Maxton delegation. The Minister of the Interior repeated in plain terms that the Spanish Government had to permit certain Communist actions because of dependence on Russian arms.

citation.quote: When another delegation, headed by John McGovern, MP, went to Spain in December, they got much the same answers as before, and Zugazagoitia, the Minister of the Interior, repeated Prieto's hint in even plainer terms. 'We have received aid from Russia and have had to permit certain actions which we did not like.'
